paper.title: Primary cilia-extracellular vesicle crosstalk in Alzheimer's disease: Emerging mechanisms and biomarker potential.
paper.journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association
paper.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative condition marked by cognitive decline and synaptic issues. Recent studies show primary cilia (PCs), sensory organelles present on the surface of most mammalian cells, act as a critical regulators of brain homeostasis and signaling. PCs act as a signaling hubs for pathways like G protein-coupled receptor, Hedgehog, Wnt, and neuroinflammation. When PCs are depleted or dysfunctional, they impair the processing of amyloid precursor protein, tau phosphorylation, synaptic signaling, and neuron-glia communication, leading to tau tangles, neuroinflammation, and amyloid beta plaques that drive AD progression. Beyond their role in signal transduction, PCs also regulate the biogenesis, release, and cargo selection of extracellular vesicles (EVs), and dysfunctional EV-PC crosstalk may contribute to AD progression. Examining PC-derived EVs offers pathway-specific insights into early ciliary and neuroinflammatory issues. This review consolidates evidence on PCs' multifaceted role in AD pathogenesis and suggests their potential as an early biomarker.
paper.full_text:
Background
Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder marked by synaptic dysfunction, neuronal loss, and cognitive decline as a result of extracellular amyloid beta (Aβ) plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) and alteration in neuronal physiological function. 1 2 Disease progression is due to excessive accumulation of oligomerized Aß, mainly due to an imbalance between its production and clearance, playing a significant role in the etiology of AD. 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 Aβ is a 4‐kDa peptide derivative of amyloid precursor protein (APP) primarily synthesized by neurons in the central nervous system (CNS), and its clearance is enabled by non‐neuronal cells like microglia and astrocytes. 7 , 8 Disease progression and pathogenicity are due to the aggregation of Aβ42 peptides produced by two proteases, beta‐site APP cleaving enzyme 1 (BACE1) and γ‐secretase, on the APP, which interrupt neural circuits. 9 , 10 Late‐onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) accounts for more than 70% of all dementia cases in people over the age of 65. 11 While Aβ plaques and NFTs remain defining neuropathological features, converging evidence from human biomarker studies and experimental models indicates that molecular and signaling abnormalities precede these lesions by years or decades. 1 , 2 This recognition has driven a shift toward biologically grounded disease frameworks and underscores the need to identify upstream regulators of neuronal homeostasis that operate early in the disease continuum and may yield mechanistically informative biomarkers. Neurons interact with one another via a complex network of axons and dendrites; however, emerging research studies indicate that neurons may detect and react to their environment through a particular organelle known as a primary cilium (PC). 12

PC is a solitary, microtubule‐based organelle present on nearly all neurons and glial cells in the mammalian brain. 13 , 14 PC consists of an axoneme featuring nine peripheral doublet microtubules that extends from a basal body (a modified centriole) and is encased within the ciliary membrane. 15 PCs are commonly identified by several ciliary markers, including adenosine diphosphate (ADP)‐ribosylation factor‐like GTPase 13B (ARL13B; a membrane‐associated small GTPase), acetylated α‐Tubulin (a modified microtubule), and adenylate cyclase 3 (ADCY3, a signaling protein enriched in the ciliary membrane). 16 , 17 , 18 PC assembly, maintenance, and bidirectional cargo trafficking are regulated by the intraflagellar transport (IFT) system, which involves IFT complex proteins such as IFT88 (IFT‐B, anterograde) and IFT140 (IFT‐B, retrograde). 19 , 20

Far from being vestigial structures, PCs function as specialized signaling hubs that integrate extracellular cues and coordinate intracellular responses critical for neuronal survival, metabolism, and plasticity. 21 , 22 By clustering distinct signaling receptors, effectors, and second messenger systems within a confined compartment, PCs allow for signal transduction that is spatially and physiologically different from dendritic or synaptic signaling. 23 , 24 , 25

RESEARCH IN CONTEXT
Systematic review: The authors reviewed the literature using traditional databases (e.g., PubMed), abstracts, and presentations to consolidate the emerging role of PCs in brain signaling, neuroinflammation, and EV biology in AD. Interpretation: This review highlights PCs’ role in brain homeostasis and cellular signaling, including their influence on EV biogenesis, release, and cargo selection. Disruption of PC or PC–EV communication may contribute to AD progression. We propose that PC‐derived EVs (cEVs) could serve as an early biomarker for the detection of preclinical AD. Future directions: Overall, this review captures the role of PCs and cEVs in AD and outlines a future‐oriented biomarker workflow that uses sequential immunocapture of CNS‐specific cEVs to identify pathway‐specific signaling dysfunction. Further studies are required to validate the clinical utility and biomarker potential of PCs and cEVs in AD.

Signaling overlap with AD
Notably, many signaling pathways centralized within PCs overlap directly with pathways implicated in AD pathogenesis, including APP processing, tau phosphorylation and cytoskeletal regulation, insulin and insulin‐like growth factor‐1 (IGF‐1) signaling, mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) activity, Wnt and Hedgehog (Hh) signaling, G protein‐coupled receptor (GPCR) pathways, and neuroinflammatory responses mediated by glial cells 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 (Table 1). Disruption of ciliary structure or signaling, often described as a ciliopathy‐like state, has been reported in multiple AD‐relevant models and appears to occur early, prior to overt plaque deposition or widespread neurodegeneration. 26 , 30 , 31 , 32 These observations position PCs upstream of classical neuropathological hallmarks and suggest that ciliary dysfunction may contribute causally to the earliest stages of disease initiation rather than representing a downstream consequence of neurodegeneration.

Ciliary marker levels correlate with cognitive hallmarks
Researchers are exploring the role of PCs in brain cells because of their significant association with CNS disorders. Aberration in PC formation or activity are associated with AD, contributing to the accumulation of NFTs, neuroinflammation, and Aβ plaques, which are the hallmarks of the disease. 33 Involvement of PCs in Sonic Hedgehog (SHH), Notch, PDGF, cAMP/GPCR, and Wnt signaling pathways underscores their significance in both neuronal activity and glial cell responses associated with AD. 15 , 34 , 35 , 36 Additionally, the dysfunction or depletion of ciliary structures in the CNS leads to significant ciliary disorders, with cognitive impairment being a common manifestation in humans, often associated with AD. 37 , 38 Disruption of these signaling pathways due to dysfunctional PCs lead to the development of neurodevelopmental disorders such as Joubert syndrome, Meckel syndrome, and Bardet‐Biedl syndrome, which are collectively classified as ciliopathies. 30 , 39 Patients with ciliopathies exhibit various neurological diseases, including cognitive impairments and behavioral abnormalities, underscoring the significance of PCs function in the brain. 40

Ciliary receptors as modulators of memory and learning
PCs are necessary to develop synaptic connections in hippocampal dentate granule neurons 41 and in interneuronal circuits 42 and serve as signaling hubs transducing extracellular cues for brain growth, cell proliferation, and neurogenesis. 43 , 44 The ciliary membrane is continuous with the cell membrane with various receptors that are embedded in it, such as the p75NTR receptor, 45 , 46 the somatostatin type 3 receptor (SSTR3), 47 , 48 , 49 and the SHH system's smoothened (SMO) and Patched (Ptch) proteins, 50 , 51 , 52 and signals from these receptors trigger numerous processes like neurogenesis, neuroblast maturation, synaptic plasticity, and memory encoding. 52 , 53 , 54 Consistent with this, mouse models lacking MCHR1 or 5‐HT6 exhibited impaired learning and memory, 55 , 56 indicating cilia‐localized receptors as essential modulators for memory and learning.

Cilia as secretory organelles: emerging roles and mechanisms
Besides signal transduction, PCs are also dynamic secretory organelles and regulate the biogenesis, release, and cargo selection of extracellular vesicles (EVs), including small EVs, that is, exosomes. 57 , 58 , 59 Through tightly regulated ectocytosis at the ciliary tip or along the ciliary shaft, they release a distinct population of EVs, commonly referred to as ciliary EVs (cEVs). 60 , 61 cEVs carry highly curated, compartment‐specific cargo that reflects the unique molecular composition and signaling state of the cilium. Their release is responsive to ligand engagement, metabolic status, mechanical stress, and cellular signaling dynamics, enabling rapid communication between cells and their microenvironment. 62 Research studies indicate that dysfunctional EV–PC crosstalk may contribute to AD progression, although the precise functions of these cells remain incompletely understood. 28 , 63 In the context of AD, where signaling dysregulation and synaptic dysfunction precede irreversible neuronal loss, cEVs may encode earlier and more causally informative molecular signatures than conventional EVs derived from specific brain cells. Given the central role of PCs in integrating AD‐relevant signaling pathways and their capacity to release biologically specialized EVs, we propose that cEVs represent an underexplored but potentially informative EV subtype in AD.

The objective of this review is to focus on cEVs in AD‐relevant contexts and to evaluate their molecular cargo as a readout of early cilia‐centered signaling dysfunction. By focusing on a defined EV population linked to an upstream regulatory organelle, this work aims to advance mechanistic understanding of preclinical AD pathogenesis and to inform the development of biologically grounded EV‐based biomarkers.

PC SIGNALING AND ITS ROLE IN AD
PC signaling pathways such as SHH and Wnt pathways have been indicated to play a role in advancing neurodegenerative disorders. 64 EVs shed from PCs regulate ciliary signaling pathways by carrying signaling molecules such as SHH and Wnt to target cells, thereby promoting downstream signaling processes. 29 , 65 Aberration of these signaling pathways during neurodegeneration may impede not only fundamental ciliary functions but also communication between brain cells.

Hippocampal dentate granule cells have PCs on their surface with various receptors that drive diverse functions ranging from neurogenesis to maturation to memory encoding. 66 , 67 , 68 In the triple transgenic AD mouse model (3xTg‐AD), reduced PC length in hippocampal dentate granule cells was accompanied by a decline in neurogenesis with sex‐dependent differences, where male mice showed reduced neurogenesis at 9 months and female at 4 months, with maximum deficits at 12 months in both sexes. 69 , 70 These lines of evidence indicate that the lack of PC‐mediated cell proliferation leads to decreased neurogenesis with an accumulation of Aβ42 and mutant tau, which is critical for the advancement of AD 69 , 71 , 72 (Figure 1).

Cilia‐dependent SHH signaling in AD
SHH signaling is one of the significant developmental pathways involved in neurogenesis and cellular differentiation and has been increasingly associated with AD. 73 , 74 PC‐mediated SHH signaling regulates hippocampal neurogenesis, 66 , 67 and the neural stem cell (NSC)/glial precursor cell (GPC) pool in the hippocampus is regulated by SHH signaling. 75 He et al. demonstrated that hippocampal regions of APP23 mice and AD patients exhibited upregulation of SHH pathway activators (SHH, SMO, and the transcriptional activators Gli1 and Gli2) and downregulation of patched receptors (Ptch1, Ptch2) and transcriptional repressor Gli3. 75 This shift reflects a loss of critical regulatory constraints normally imposed by PCs, resulting in unbuffered SHH signaling. In addition, exposure of isolated hippocampal GPCs to a high dose of Aβ42 markedly reduced Ptch and Gli expression while elevating SHH expression. 75 Deficits of Ptch1–Gli1 signaling induced NSCs/GPCs into asymmetric division, leading to an increase in dividing cells, leading to apoptosis‐like death, depleting the adult neural precursor cell pool and defective neurogenesis. 75 Functionally, reduced Ptch–Gli3 signaling drives NSCs and GPCs toward excessive asymmetric division, producing a transient increase in proliferating cells followed by replication stress, apoptosis‐like cell death, and depletion of the adult neural precursor pool. 75 Another study reinforced the notion that loss of ciliary regulatory control underlies aberrant SHH signaling, where Aβ accumulation disrupted primary ciliogenesis and impaired the SHH signaling system by preventing GPCs from expressing Ptch1 and Gli1. 76 These findings suggest that PC signaling dysregulation results in the depletion of the GPC pool, impacting neuronal development and contributing to cognitive decline in AD. 77

Consistent with this maladaptive signaling model, pharmacological inhibition of SHH signaling using protease nexin‐1 or the smoothened antagonist cyclopamine reduces hippocampal neuronal apoptosis and improves spatial learning and memory in AD mouse models. 78 Collectively, these findings suggest that SHH signaling becomes pathogenic when uncoupled from proper PC‐mediated regulation, positioning PC dysfunction upstream of impaired neurogenesis and cognitive decline in AD. These findings underscore the importance of restoring physiological ciliary signaling dynamics rather than indiscriminately activating the SHH pathway.

Cilia‐associated Wnt signaling in AD
Wnt signaling plays a central role in neuronal development, synaptic plasticity, and neuroprotection, and accumulating evidence indicates that PCs are critical regulators of Wnt pathway organization and signal fidelity. 14 , 79 , 80 EVs released from Wnt‐expressing cells deliver Wnt proteins to PC, promoting the recruitment of signaling components and thereby linking ciliary integrity to Wnt activating downstream processes. 81 , 82 , 83 Dysregulation of cilia‐mediated Wnt signaling has been linked to the pathophysiology of AD. 84 , 85

Several research studies showed increased glycogen synthase kinase 3β (GSK3β) activity and decreased β‐catenin levels in AD brains. 86 , 87 , 88 , 89 Furthermore, Wnt signaling is impaired in AD brain cortical regions through induction of Dickkopf‐1 (DKK1), a negative modulator of WNT signaling that activates the tau‐phosphorylating enzyme GSK3β. 90 In line with these findings, age‐related downregulation of WNT ligands, including WNT2b, WNT6, WNT7a, WNT2, WNT3, WNT3a, WNT4, and WNT9a, along with reduced expression of frizzled receptors FZD2 and FZD3 and transcription factors LEF1 and TCF3, has been shown in the aging human brain and rodent models. 91 , 92 , 93 , 94 Together, loss of Wnt/β‐catenin signaling contributes to AD‐like pathology and highlighting the role of Wnt pathway disruption in neurodegeneration. 91 , 92

Interestingly, pharmacological activation of Wnt/β‐catenin signaling restores synaptic integrity and cognitive function in AD mouse models. Vargas et al. found that intrahippocampal administration of WASP‐1 (Wnt‐activating small molecule potentiator‐1), a Wnt/β‐catenin activator, restored synaptic impairments in APP/presenilin 1 (PS1) mice. 95 Thus, Wnt signaling may be a therapeutically tractable pathway whose pathological impact may arise from disrupted ciliary regulation rather than uniform pathway suppression.

Notch signaling in AD
Notch signaling is a spatially regulated pathway whose activity depends on precise subcellular organization, including localization to PCs and periciliary membranes, which act as signaling hubs constraining Notch receptor trafficking, endocytosis, and γ‐secretase–mediated processing. 96 , 97 , 98 Notch signaling plays a substantial role in neurodevelopment, adult neurogenesis, and synaptic plasticity, exerting tight control over cell fate determination and the balance between NSC proliferation and differentiation in coordination with Wnt signaling. 99 , 100 , 101 , 102 , 103 Canonical Notch activation requires sequential proteolytic processing, culminating in γ‐secretase–mediated release of the Notch intracellular domain (NICD), which translocates to the nucleus to regulate transcription. Notably, γ‐secretase also cleaves APP to generate Aβ, establishing a mechanistic intersection between Notch signaling and AD pathogenesis. 99 , 104 , 105 , 106 Genetic and experimental evidence further supports this link as presenilins, core components of the γ‐secretase complex, interact with both Notch and APP in postmitotic neurons, and mutations in APP and PS1 and PS2 cause early‐onset AD. 104 , 107 , 108 PS1 and PS1/PS2 deletion mice exhibit similar phenotypes to Notch knockouts, 109 , 110 and knockouts of γ‐secretase components cause developmental abnormalities like Notch 1 and Notch 2 knockouts. 111 , 112

In AD, Notch signaling is impaired in both directions. AD patients show reduced levels of full‐length and truncated Notch1 in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), indicating its aberrant accumulation in the brain parenchyma. 113 Abnormal Notch activation in AD models has been shown to directly impact Aβ plaque development and clearance of Aβ plaques, 106 while loss of Notch function exhibits AD‐like neuronal dysfunction and spatial memory deficits. 114 , 115 Collectively, these findings suggest that dysregulated Notch processing, rather than absolute pathway activity, drives pathology in a highly context‐dependent manner.

The context dependence of Notch in AD is further supported by experimental evidence. Intraperitoneal injection of the c‐jun‐NH2‐terminal kinase (JNK) inhibitor SP600125 reduced Notch1 signaling in C57BL/6 mice without triggering apoptosis, 116 and chronic SP600125 treatment reduced amyloid plaque burden, Aβ production, and tau hyperphosphorylation in an AD mouse model. 117 Simultaneously, intragastrically administered curcumin stimulates the Notch signaling pathway in 9‐month‐old AD mice, promoting the proliferation of adult neural stem cells and neuronal differentiation. 118 These studies suggested that partial suppression of Notch signaling reduces Aβ and tau pathology, whereas controlled Notch activation promotes adult neurogenesis and neuronal differentiation, highlighting the need for therapeutic strategies that restore physiological Notch signaling dynamics rather than indiscriminately enhancing or inhibiting the pathway.

Further, accumulating evidence indicates that PCs and EV trafficking act as essential regulators of Notch signaling fidelity. Aβ‐associated disruption of ciliogenesis and vesicular trafficking may impair the spatial regulation, leading to abnormal Notch processing and dysregulated γ‐secretase activity. 119 , 120 , 121 Given that γ‐secretase is shared by both Notch and APP, ciliary dysfunction may simultaneously perturb Notch‐dependent regulation of neurogenesis and synaptic maintenance while promoting amyloidogenic APP cleavage. The Notch pathway is additionally tightly coupled to ligand‐induced receptor internalization and endosomal trafficking, which intersect with EV pathways known to be disrupted in AD. 119 , 120 , 121 Notably, EVs have been shown to carry Notch receptors, ligands, and γ‐secretase components, enabling intercellular propagation of Notch signaling states and potentially amplifying dysregulated signaling in disease. 122 , 123 This framework provides a mechanistic basis for observations that both inhibition and activation of Notch signaling can confer benefit in AD models, depending on timing, cellular context, and degree of pathway disruption. 66 , 121 , 124 Collectively, these findings position cilia‐associated Notch dysregulation as a potential upstream contributor to maladaptive neurogenesis, synaptic failure, and Aβ pathology in AD and candidate therapeutic and biomarker target.

TGF‐β signaling in AD
The pathophysiology of AD is additionally influenced by impaired transforming growth factor‐beta (TGF‐β) signaling. Clinical studies have shown elevated levels of TGF‐β1 in CSF and Aβ plaques with reduced levels in plasma, suggesting dysregulated compartment‐specific signaling in AD individuals. 125 , 126 , 127 , 128 , 129 Reduced expression of TGF‐βRII (TGF‐beta type II receptor) and impaired Smad3 signaling are associated with increased Aβ accumulation, NFT formation, and neurodegeneration. 130 , 131 , 132 Downstream consequences of impaired TGF‐β/Smad signaling leads to defective Smad phosphorylation, tau hyperphosphorylation, increased astroglial reactivity, microgliosis, neuronal cell cycle reactivation, decreased Aβ clearance, and the development of cerebral amyloid angiopathy. 133 , 134 , 135 , 136 , 137

Despite these findings, the role of TGF‐β1 in AD remains debated due to conflicting results. TGF‐β1 induces APP gene expression in various cell cultures, potentially increasing Aβ production, 126 , 138 and its overexpression in transgenic AD mice accelerates Aβ deposition in cerebral blood vessels, leading to AD‐like vascular alterations and inflammatory processes. 139 , 140 Conversely, blocking of TGF‐β‐Smad 2/3 reduces Aβ deposits and abundance, promoting Smad1/5/8 signaling and increased Aβ‐containing macrophage‐mediated Aβ clearance. 141 Aged transgenic mice with increased astroglial TGF‐β1 production exhibit lower hippocampal and dystrophic neurite Aβ burdens. 142 Overall, the evidence indicates that TGF‐ß1 decreases parenchymal Aβ accumulation while increasing Aβ deposition in cerebral blood vessels 143 and that TGF‐β signaling plays a complex, context‐dependent role in AD, contributing to neurodegeneration while also exerting neurotrophic and neuroprotective effects that support neuronal survival. 143

Further, emerging evidence suggests that TGF‐β dysregulation may be mediated, in part, by PCs and cEVs. PCs act as specialized signaling organelles in brain cells, serving as hubs for pathways critical to brain homeostasis, including TGF‐β/Smad signaling, and endocytosis. 21 , 144 Disruption of ciliary structure or intraflagellar trafficking, which has been increasingly reported in neurodegenerative disorders, 27 , 40 may impair proper localization of TGF‐β receptors and downstream Smad activation, thereby contributing to tau hyperphosphorylation, neuronal cell‐cycle re‐entry, and neuroinflammation observed in AD. Moreover, ciliary dysfunction may modify cEV composition and receptor trafficking, thereby altering the spatial distribution of TGF‐β ligands and receptor complexes between parenchymal and vascular compartments.

A unifying explanation for these apparently contradictory findings is that TGF‐β signaling in AD may diverge depending on whether it is engaged within the specialized microdomain of the PC or through non‐ciliary bulk plasma membrane receptors. Ciliary‐localized TGF‐β receptors may preferentially couple to canonical Smad2/3 signaling in neurons, supporting cytostatic, homeostatic, and neuroprotective programs that enhance Aβ clearance and maintain synaptic stability. 21 , 144 In contrast, mislocalization of TGF‐β receptors away from the ciliary compartment due to impaired IFT, altered endocytosis, or structural ciliary loss may shift signaling toward non‐canonical pathways (e.g., MAPK, PI3K/AKT, or pro‐fibrotic cascades) in astrocytes, microglia, or vascular cells, promoting APP upregulation, vascular Aβ deposition, gliosis, and inflammatory amplification. Additionally, intact ciliary TGF‐β signaling supports neuroprotection and parenchymal Aβ restraint, whereas disrupted or extraciliary TGF‐β signaling favors vascular deposition, inflammatory remodeling, and pathogenic Aβ accumulation. Integrating ciliary context into TGF‐β biology therefore provides a coherent framework to reconcile its dual protective and deleterious roles in AD.

CILIARY DYSFUNCTION AS A CONTRIBUTOR TO AMYLOID‐ β ACCUMULATION
Aβ accumulation is fundamental to the pathogenesis of AD and serves as the basis for the amyloid cascade theory. 145 , 146 According to research findings, APP is localized to PCs and plays a vital role in ciliogenesis and brain development. 77 , 147 Emerging studies have shown PCs are involved in endocytosis and release EVs containing Aβ, and aberrant PCs promote excessive EV release loaded with Aβ, contributing to AD pathology. 63 , 148 Dysfunctional cilia lead to abnormal APP processing and encourage the buildup of toxic Aβ, 77 , 149 and altered cilia length negatively impacts synaptic connection and neuronal morphology. 42 , 150 , 151 Another study showed impaired ciliary dynamics in the APP knock‐in mouse model (AppNL‐G‐F ), with an increase in ciliary length in the DG but not in the CA1 and CA3 regions in which greater Aβ was accumulated. 149 In line with this, exposure to Aβ42 in hTERT‐RPE1 cells and dissociated rat hippocampal neurons results in reduced cilia length, 149 and accumulation of Aβ42 in mouse NIH3T3 cells results in a significant reduction in PC length and frequency, collectively indicating that extracellular Aβ negatively impacts PC dynamics. 77 Additionally, accumulated Aβ impairs both steady‐state and agonist‐induced canonical SHH signaling, likely due to abnormal cilia assembly and maintenance. 52 , 66 , 77 , 152

PC DYSFUNCTION AND TAU PROTEIN ACCUMULATION
In AD, tau proteins undergo aberrant phosphorylation, leading to the formation of NFTs and neuronal impairment/dysfunction. 153 , 154 cEVs facilitate tau protein accumulation by serving as carriers that distribute tau pathology between cells, thereby contributing to its propagation. 155 , 156 , 157 Tau tubulin kinase 2 (TTBK2) is a key regulator of PC formation initiation and maintenance through regulation of ciliary gate components and IFT. 158 Conditional knockout of TTBK2 in adult mice results in degenerative cerebellar phenotypes similar to those seen in spinocerebellar ataxia type 11 (SCA11), demonstrating that TTBK2 is required not only for ciliogenesis but also for long‐term neuronal maintenance. 159 Consistent with this, loss of the IFT protein IFT88 from the adult brain results in impaired ciliary structure and defects in cerebellar architecture and locomotor behavior similar to those observed in animals lacking TTBK2, indicating that intact PC signaling is critical for neuronal survival and circuit integrity. 159 Additionally, tau protein is known to be phosphorylated by TTBK2, linking ciliary regulation to tau biology. Disruption of TTBK2 activity may therefore promote aberrant tau phosphorylation, facilitating the formation of neurotoxic tau species and aggregates characteristic of AD and other tauopathies. 160 Furthermore, impaired TTBK2‐dependent ciliogenesis may disrupt ciliary control of EV docking, uptake, or release, potentially enhancing the intercellular spread of phosphorylated or misfolded tau in a non‐cell‐autonomous manner.

The intersection of the PC—EV–tau axis represents a largely untapped area of investigation in AD. While aberrant tau phosphorylation, aggregation into NFTs, and EV‐mediated tau propagation are well‐established components of AD pathology, these processes have rarely been examined within the framework of ciliary signaling. Key mechanistic questions remain largely unaddressed, that is, whether ciliary dysfunction alters the subcellular distribution of tau kinases or phosphatases, thereby shifting tau toward aggregation‐prone states, and whether ciliary structural integrity influences EV cargo remodeling in tauopathy contexts. If ciliary dysfunction precedes or amplifies tau pathology, cilia‐associated EV signatures could serve as early biomarkers of tau dysregulation before overt tangle formation, a potential clinical implication that heightens the urgency of experimental investigation.

It is crucial to note that PC remodeling in AD is context‐dependent and specific to cell type. Although PCs have been observed in astrocytes and oligodendrocyte lineage cells of the CNS, research on the role of glial cilia is still in the early stages. 27 , 161 , 162 , 163 Consequently, the subsequent sections will investigate the distinct manifestations of PC dysfunction and cEV‐mediated signaling in neuronal, astrocytic, and oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC) populations in the context of AD.

PCs IN NEURONAL CELLS
PCs play a critical role in regulating neurogenesis, cell polarity, axonal guidance, and adult neuronal function. 37 PC‐mediated Shh signaling facilitates neurogenesis in the cerebellum and hippocampus, as well as the proliferation of granule neuronal progenitor pools. 66 , 164 Neuronal PCs are enriched with type 3 adenylyl cyclase (AC3), indicating their role as specialized signaling compartments. 12 In neuronal cells, ciliary GPCRs act as extrasynaptic receptors that sense neuromodulators in the local environment, transducing signals through AC3 and downstream cAMP‐dependent cascades, with AC3 being highly enriched in neuronal cilia of the hippocampus and cortex. 165 PCs in hippocampal neurons also form axo‐ciliary synapses with brainstem axons and serve as essential hubs for Hh and Wnt signaling pathways, which are vital for neuronal polarity, cell fate determination, and tissue patterning. 166

Emerging evidence suggests that dysfunction of neuronal PCs contribute to the pathogenesis of AD and any alterations in PC morphology, including abnormal changes in ciliary length and frequency reported in AD models and are associated with impaired neuronal signaling and reduced neurogenic capacity. 26 , 29 , 149 In the App NL‐G‐F knock‐in mouse model of AD, hippocampal neurons exhibited disrupted age‐dependent ciliary elongation in regions with high Aβ deposition, suggesting a direct relationship between amyloid pathology and neuronal PC dysfunction. 149 PCs also regulate autophagy and intracellular protein homeostasis, raising the possibility that neuronal ciliary dysfunction may exacerbate the accumulation of toxic Aβ and tau aggregates during disease progression. 167 Age‐dependent elongation of AC3‐ and MCHR1‐positive primary cilia has been observed in rat and mouse hippocampal CA1, CA3, and dentate gyrus neurons, 39 , 168 , 169 indicating that baseline ciliary dynamics in these areas are especially susceptible to age‐related and pathological disturbances.

In addition to functioning as signal receivers, PCs also actively secrete EVs. Ciliary mutant neurons demonstrate increased secretion of small EVs with an altered cargo composition, and these EVs are biologically active, modulating the WNT response in recipient cells implicating ciliary EV release as a key mechanism by which cilia regulate intercellular signaling. 170 Activated ciliary GPCRs can accumulate at the ciliary tip and be released in EVs called ectosomes, raising the possibility that ciliary GPCR signals may be transmitted between cells via vesicular carriers. 21 In AD, this cilia–EV axis becomes critically dysregulated. Disruption of PCs through knockdown of the IFT gene Ift88 in primary hippocampal neurons reduces CD63‐positive EV release, resulting in intracellular Aβ accumulation and enhanced extracellular Aβ uptake, demonstrating that PCs are necessary for EV‐mediated Aβ clearance. 26 In AD mouse models, dystrophic neurites formed from synaptic loss due to ectopic EV accumulation at axon terminals are linked to PC dysfunction. Consistent with this, single‐cell RNA sequencing showed that septal‐projecting hippocampal somatostatin neurons are vulnerable to Aβ‐related cilia impairment and vesicle buildup. 63 In the broader AD context, EVs carrying pathogenic forms of Aβ and phosphorylated tau are internalized by both local and distant neurons, contributing to the propagation of AD pathology and exacerbating neuronal degeneration. 171 Collectively, anomalies in PC function and morphology, particularly their regulation of EV biogenesis and secretion, are closely linked to key AD pathologies, and further studies on neuronal cilia dynamics during aging and neurodegeneration are essential to evaluate their potential as therapeutic targets. 26

PCs IN GLIAL CELLS: ROLE IN NEUROINFLAMMATION
Glial cells are the primary constituents of the nervous system and are essential for neural development, homeostasis, and neurological conditions. Various types of glial cells exist in the nervous system, including astrocytes, microglial cells, oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells, and olfactory ensheathing cells. 172 , 173 , 174 The existence of PCs havebeen reported in astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and Schwann cells of the CNS and peripheral nervous system; however, the functional significance of glial cilia is not completely understood. 175 , 176 , 177

PCs in microglial cells and neuroinflammatory signaling
Microglial cells are the primary immune cells involved in brain development and homeostasis, removing dead cells, cellular debris, and synaptic debris, including Aβ, from the brain. 178 They secrete cytokines and chemokines and play a role in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases like AD. 179 In AD, activated microglia, also known as disease‐associated microglia (DAM) or neurodegeneration microglia (MGnD), are attracted to Aβ plaques and exhibit increased phagocytosis of Aβ and dystrophic neurites. 180 , 181 However, the phagocytic capacity of microglia is eventually exhausted, and phagocytic cells release undegraded Aβ after lysosomal concentration, which limits damage and serves as a seed for extracellular Aβ plaques and neurite dystrophy. 182 Phagocytosis of extracellular debris results in creating phagolysosomes, which progressively weaken the degradative capacity of lysosomes and increase the phagocytic activity by utilizing lysosomal hydrolases. 183 , 184

Activated microglia highly expresses genes responsible for EV production and release disease associated EVs that contribute to AD pathology. 180 , 181 Disease‐associated microglia encapsulate and disperse phosphorylated tau in TSG101‐positive EVs, 155 while microglial EVs generated during pro‐inflammatory conditions are enriched with complement proteins, cytokines, and tau aggregates. 185 , 186 EVs are discharged from intracellular endosomal recycling via lysosomes and multivesicular bodies with lysosomal exocytosis tightly regulated by small GTPases, transcription factor EB (TFEB), and lysosomal proteins and enzymes. 187 , 188 , 189 EV release pathways are closely linked to lysosomal function, playing a critical role in preventing lysosomal storage failure and toxic intracellular accumulation. 190 , 191 , 192 Wnt signaling stimulation further activates microglia increasing pro‐inflammatory EV release. 185 , 186

PCs transiently observed on microglia in the lateral septum regulate microglial phagocytosis and Aβ exocytosis, thereby influencing extracellular proteostasis, Aβ plaque deposition, and neurite dystrophy. 148 Disruption of EV secretion, mediated by microglial PCs, significantly impacts Aβ plaques and dystrophic neurites, suggesting that genes linked to EVs may be risk factors for AD (Figure 2A). Notably, inhibition of the ciliary gene Ift88 in microglia promotes phagocytosis and the release of EVs with altered proteomic composition, resulting in aberrant extracellular proteostasis and neurite degeneration in an AD mouse model. 148 Therefore, emphasizing the microglial PC signaling pathway may be an effective approach to regulating neuroimmune responses in AD therapies.

PC‐mediated signaling in astrocytes
Astrocytes, the predominant glial cells in the CNS, are essential for the formation and maintenance of the blood—brain barrier and for secreting numerous neurotrophic factors throughout synaptogenesis, differentiation, and survival. 193 , 194 Astrocytic cilia are essential for CNS development and pathology, as they harbor SHH signaling molecules such as SMO and PTCH1 177 , 195 , 196 , 197 (Table 1).

Recent studies suggest that in AD, reactive astrocytes exacerbate neurodegenerative processes by enhancing neurotoxicity via the production of inflammatory cytokines, including reactive oxygen species (ROS), and inflammatory mediators, including COX2, IL‐1β, TNF‐α, and IL‐6. 198 These inflammatory mediators disrupt the assembly and length regulation of PC, thereby impairing the SHH signaling and contributing to neuron degeneration 77 , 198 , 199 , 200 (Figure 2A).

In the hippocampal subgranular zone (SGZ), astrocyte‐like type 1 radial glial cells generate new granule cells for memory encoding. 49 , 201 These cells exhibit characteristics of astrocytes, including glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and feature non‐motile PCs encased in a plasma membrane rich in receptors such as p75NTR, 45 , 202 SSTR3, 47 , 48 and SMO and PTCH proteins of the SHH signaling pathway. 51 , 52 Signals from these cilia facilitate vital functions like neurogenesis, neuroblast development, and memory encoding. Neurotrophin‐mediated p75NTR signaling stimulates the proliferation of granule cell precursors in the dentate gyrus subventricular zone, 49 , 53 , 201 whereas SSTR3 and SHH signaling regulates hippocampal neurogenesis and excitatory synaptic signals. 66 , 203

In the brains of AD individuals, accumulated toxic Aβ42 oligomers promote the proliferation of granule cell progenitors, but when trapped in fibrillary plaques, these progenitor cells fail to mature or survive, resulting in ineffective neurogenesis. 204 , 205 , 206 This arrested maturation is likely driven by disrupted neuromodulatory signaling rather than a lack of progenitor proliferation per se. In particular, reduced somatostatin levels and impaired ciliary somatostatin receptor 3 (SSTR3) signaling, both of which are critical for hippocampal‐dependent memory encoding, have been consistently observed in AD. 49 , 201

EVs shed by astrocyte PCs include various internal cargoes, including proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids and regulate the brain's immune response to inflammatory cytokines, including IL‐1β. 207 , 208 In general, astrocyte‐derived EVs facilitate neurite proliferation and neuronal viability. However, during inflammatory conditions, they release EVs that adversely impact the immune response. IL‐1β‐induced astrocytic cEVs are internalized by neurons, compromising synaptic integrity and intensifying susceptibility to neurotoxins, although direct mechanistic evidence in vivo is still limited. 209 , 210 , 211

Additionally, astrocytic PCs regulate SHH signaling to facilitate progenitor cell proliferation and neuron‐astrocyte interactions, especially in neurotoxic and neuroinflammatory conditions. 22 , 196 The disruption of cilia‐dependent signaling pathways in AD may directly hinder neuronal maturation and circuit integration, indicating that cognitive decline associated with AD arises not solely from synaptic loss and neuronal death but also from a failure of cilia‐dependent regenerative signaling. 69 , 70 , 71 , 197

PCs in OPCs
Oligodendrocytes are essential for CNS myelination differentiated from OPCs, which involves securely wrapping around nerve axons and producing numerous layers of myelin. Development of functional myelin involves interactions between oligodendrocytes and neurons, with oligodendrocytes internalizing EVs from neurons for neuroprotection within the CNS 212 (Figure 2B). Impairment in oligodendrocyte function can result in neurological disorders such as AD. 213

Emerging evidence indicates that PCs are integral for OPC differentiation and the pathogenic processes involved in demyelinating disorders. Key ciliary proteins, including KIF3A and IFT 81, as well as SHH signaling elements, such as SMO and PTCH1, are present in mouse cortical OPCs, 214 , 215 and PCs undergo regulated disassembly during differentiation into mature oligodendrocytes. 176 The reduced expression of Ift88 and KIF3A impairs SHH signaling in OPCs, impeding oligodendrocyte proliferation and differentiation, resulting in motor impairments attributed to a decline in myelinated axons following white matter injury 162 , 216 , 217 (Figure 2B). Furthermore, dysregulation of PC length in OPCs hindered oligodendrocyte development. 218 , 219 Consequently, regulating ciliary biogenesis during oligodendrocyte development may serve as a viable therapeutic target for demyelinating diseases.

While EVs are known to play a role in oligodendrocyte–neuron communication, 212 the characterization of cEVs specifically originating from OPCs or mature oligodendrocytes is largely unexplored, and, to our knowledge, no studies have directly explored cilia‐derived EV release or cargo composition from this cell type. This signifies a significant gap, as ciliary signaling is essential for OPC differentiation and myelination, and cEV‐based assessments of OPC cilia disruption may offer novel biomarkers or therapeutic strategies in demyelinating disorders.

Glial cilia exhibit distinct sensory architectures during neuroinflammation
Although neuronal PCs have been comparatively well characterized, 220 the molecular composition and signaling logic of astrocytic and microglial cilia remain incompletely defined. Emerging data indicate that glial cilia are not passive remnants but active sensory hubs that tune inflammatory tone, metabolic coupling, and tissue repair. Importantly, glial ciliary GPCR repertoires appear to differ from neuronal cilia, implying cell‐type‐specific interpretation of extracellular cues in the inflamed or amyloid‐laden brain. 27 , 221

Astrocytic cilia integrate neuromodulatory and metabolic signals within tripartite synapses and perivascular niches. 222 They harbor links to cAMP signaling and calcium dynamics, potentially regulating gliotransmission, vascular coupling, and reactive state transitions. 222 , 223 Through ciliary receptors, astrocytes may sense neurotransmitter spillover or lipid mediators and convert these cues into transcriptional programs influencing complement production, cytokine release, and Aβ clearance.

Microglial cilia, though less studied, may act as immune‐sensory antennae. They contain GPCRs that detect injury signals, and ciliary localization might regulate inflammatory signaling thresholds. If immune GPCRs localize to cilia, they could create microdomains controlling pathways like Smad, cAMP, or MAPK, preventing excessive inflammation. Loss of ciliary integrity may dysregulate ligand sensitivity, pushing microglia toward chronic activation seen in AD.

From a translational perspective, defining glial‐specific ciliary GPCR signatures would refine cEV biomarker panels and enable cell‐type‐resolved inflammatory endophenotyping.

CILIARY EXTRACELLULAR VESICLES CONTRIBUTE TO AD PATHOLOGY AND SERVE AS EMERGING BIOMARKERS
EVs are membrane‐bound structures released into the extracellular space by nearly all cells. 224 EVs include exosomes, microvesicles, and apoptotic bodies distinguished by their biogenesis, release mechanism, size, composition, and roles. 225 , 226 , 227 These released EVs are categorized by their cellular origins, specifically from ciliated and non‐ciliated endothelial cells, with cEVs being distinct from cytosolic EVs. 228 The ciliary surface provides a specialized region for EV release into the extracellular environment, facilitating intercellular communication, and ciliary‐derived EVs may regulate ciliogenesis. 57 , 60 , 62 , 229 The IFT/BBSome mechanism is involved in EV sorting and release, such that ciliary aberrations may skew EV cargo toward pathogenic proteins or impair the delivery of protective trophic signals. 230

In AD, disruption in PC biogenesis or dysfunction directly affects EV‐mediated pathogenesis. Aberrant PC biogenesis or dysfunction hinders the EV‐mediated secretion of Aβ at the axon terminals. This accumulation causes synapse loss and formation of dystrophic neurites, contributing to the spread of Aβ in the brains of AD patients. 63 In accordance with this, EVs derived from AD brain, CSF, and plasma exhibit elevated levels of APP carboxy‐terminal fragments (APP‐CTF), Aβ species, and p‐tau, 157 , 231 , 232 and cilia‐associated modifications in endosomal maturation may further promote the EV‐mediated propagation of these proteopathic proteins. 63 As discussed earlier, Aβ induces structural and functional aberrations in PCs, causing cilia shortening, loss of ciliary membrane regulator ARL13B, and disrupted IFT reflected by reduced IFT88 levels, collectively impairing ciliary stability and GPCR localization. 26 , 31 , 233 Significantly, human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)‐derived neurons and cerebral organoids have demonstrated that modulation of ciliary genes, including IFT88, KIF3A, ARL13B, and BBS proteins, affects the neuronal susceptibility to Aβ and tau and modifies EV cargo composition, 234 , 235 , 236 thereby directly linking cilia–EV axis in AD‐related pathways, including APP processing, tau pathology, neuroinflammation, and endosomal–lysosomal dysfunction. 26 , 148

Endosomal–lysosomal dysregulation is a fundamental characteristic of AD and is closely associated with ciliogenesis and EV biogenesis. AD risk genes such as SORL1, BIN1, PICALM, and TREM2 modulate endosomal trafficking and may indirectly disrupt ciliary biogenesis or stability. 237 , 238 , 239 , 240 Disruption of these pathways increases the secretion of pathogenic EVs, establishing a feedback loop in which endosomal defects hinder ciliogenesis and further intensify abnormal EV release. 170 , 241 , 242 These modifications can be identified through blood‐based endosomal–cilia–EV biomarkers, which could facilitate the detection of early endosomal stress and monitor therapeutic engagement. 243

Biological rationale for studying ciliary EVs in AD
PC and EV interactions offer multiple translational avenues for AD and provide prospective targets for diagnostic biomarkers in biological fluids and therapeutic delivery systems. 244 , 245 Studies have shown that cEVs contain biomarkers (e.g., NADPH‐cytochrome P450 reductase, topoisomerase IIα, and CD151) that interact with AD proteins such as APP, peptidyl‐prolyl cis‐trans isomerase NIMA‐interacting 1 (PIN1), and cathepsin B (CTSB). 228 , 246 If cilia dysfunction in AD, the composition and quantity of cEVs they release may undergo detectable alterations, including variation in cEV abundance and proteomic content such as the depletion of canonical ciliary markers indicative of structural and functional ciliary degradation and the abnormal accumulation of AD‐associated proteins that may be the consequence of disrupted ciliary membrane integrity and disrupted cargo‐sorting mechanisms. In contrast to total EVs, which obscure cell‐type‐ and compartment‐specific signals, cEVs derive from ciliary compartment and contain cargo that is both enriched in and specific to the ciliary membrane, rendering their protein content a more direct and mechanistically interpretable indicator of ciliary functional state. Among these detectable changes, variations in the levels of ciliary proteins that were identified in neuron‐derived cEVs in vitro, including ARL13B, SSTR3, and fragments of the 5‐HT6 GPCR, 60 , 163 , 165 may serve as potential early blood‐based biomarkers as variations in their abundance within circulating EVs could indicate ciliary dysfunction in AD (Figure 3A).

In addition to their biomarker potential, ciliary trafficking pathways may serve as targets of therapeutic intervention. Restoring ciliary trafficking components such as IFT88 or BBS proteins could normalize EV release profiles and impede the propagation of tau‐ and Aβ‐laden vesicles. Likewise, EV signatures indicative of glial ciliary dysfunction (C3/C4 complement factors, cytokine‐laden EVs, and ciliary GPCR fragments) may classify inflammatory endophenotypes in AD, potentially via blood‐based assays targeting glia‐specific EVs. 185 , 247

Moreover, the intracellular accumulation of cEVs caused by ciliary dysfunction does not necessarily indicate impaired total EV secretion; rather, it reflects disrupted cilia‐associated trafficking and endolysosomal processing that selectively alters specific EV subpopulations. 59 , 63 , 228 , 248 , 249 , 250 In accordance with this notion, compounds such as TFEB activators or mTOR inhibitors that stimulate lysosomal activity may restore ciliary integrity, enhance EV‐lysosomal flux, and reduce pathogenic cEV cargo accumulation (Figure 3B).

Notably, several AD risk genes, which include SORL1, BIN1, PICALM, and TREM2, regulate endosomal vesicle trafficking through molecular machinery that is shared with ciliary transport systems, 240 especially involving the retromer complex, 251 the BBSome‐associated transport, and Rab GTPase‐dependent cargo sorting. 252 Since the composition of cEV cargo directly reflects the state of this shared trafficking network, 246 tracking changes in cEV cargo may serve as an accessible blood‐based pharmacodynamic readout to verify target engagement when therapies directed at these genes are administered.

cEV as next‐generation biomarkers
cEVs represent a compelling next‐generation biomarker class for AD because they can report upstream, pathway‐specific signaling dysfunction that likely emerges during prodromal and even preclinical stages, that is, well before aggregates and injury‐based readouts dominate. PC concentrates key signaling machinery within a restricted membrane domain, making cEV cargo intrinsically less diluted and more mechanistically interpretable than bulk EV preparations. Priority protein candidates encompass four functional categories. Cilia‐localized GPCRs, such as SSTR3, MCHR1, and 5‐HT6, indicate impaired ciliary receptor signaling. Second, IFT and BBSome proteins function as markers for ciliary trafficking defects. Third, APP‐processing regulators linked to ciliary microdomains, along with tau‐modifying kinases and phosphatases localized in ciliary signaling compartments, establish direct connections to AD pathogenesis. Ultimately, inflammation‐associated receptors on neuronal and glial cilia link ciliary dysfunction to neuroinflammatory pathways. Furthermore, the distinct ciliary lipidome, which is defined by phosphoinositide enrichment and cholesterol‐sensitive microdomains, 253 , 254 , 255 may amplify AD‐relevant lipid dysregulation for earlier detection.

Development of blood‐based assays for cEVs
In AD science, CSF and blood‐based biomarkers provide a high‐yield matrix for discovery and mechanistic validation. Within blood‐based techniques, cEV assays are especially attractive for scalable screening and longitudinal monitoring, provided that cEVs can be robustly enriched. To address the rarity and cell‐type specificity of cEVs, a proposed practical approach is sequential immunocapture from plasma.

Sequential immunocapture can be implemented in two hypothesis‐driven idealized configurations (Figure 4). In a specificity‐first (CNS→ciliary) workflow, EV‐rich size‐exclusion chromatography fractions are first immunocaptured for CNS origin (e.g., L1CAM for neuron‐derived EVs, 256 GLAST for astrocyte‐derived EVs, 257 TMEM119 for microglia‐derived EVs 258 ), and these CNS‐enriched EV pools are then subjected to a second capture for ciliary identity (e.g., ARL13B and/or ADCY3, 16 , 259 optionally supplemented by validated ciliary GPCR ectodomain reagents such as SSTR3 259 or 5‐HT6 260 ). Conversely, in a yield‐first (ciliary→CNS) workflow, total EV preparations are first enriched for ciliary‐marked vesicles (ARL13B/ADCY3 ± ciliary GPCR capture), and the resulting cEV‐enriched pool is subsequently fractionated by CNS origin using L1CAM/GLAST/TMEM119 immunocapture. Together, these two configurations provide an adaptable trade‐off between brain specificity and recovery of low‐abundance cEVs.

Since plasma‐derived cEV isolation and enrichment methods in the context of AD has not been explored to our knowledge, the enriched cEV populations would require extensive characterization using electron microscopy, single‐EV flow cytometry, and nanoparticle tracking analysis. The main objective of downstream analyses is to identify cEV‐associated biomarkers that emerge early during AD progression. This may involve the use of ultrasensitive biomarker quantification platforms, such as single‐molecule array (Simoa by Quanterix), Meso Scale Discovery, and liquid chromatography‐tandem mass spectrometry.

Benchmarking cEV biomarkers against established blood biomarkers for AD
Translationally, cEV biomarkers can be integrated into the amyloid (A), tau (T), and neurodegeneration (N) framework 261 by positioning them as an upstream, pathway‐resolved layer that reports mechanistic vulnerability before the canonical signals are clearly abnormal. While A/T/N is optimized for classifying established AD pathophysiology (Aβ deposition, tau pathology, and downstream injury), whereas cEV could indicate a conceptual “Stage 0” state capturing early ciliary/endolysosomal trafficking stress, GPCR mislocalization, and inflammatory priming that biases the system toward later A/T/N positivity. In practical terms, cEV readouts would not replace A/T/N biomarker framework; rather, they would extend it earlier in time by adding a pre‐A/T/N stratum that identifies individuals at risk of transitioning toward amyloid positivity (A+) and/or tau positivity (T+) trajectories.

To validate this pre‐A/T/N stratum, biomarkers that distinctively indicate early ciliary disruption are required. cEV markers like ARL13B, ciliary GPCRs (e.g., SSTR3, 5‐HT6, GPR161), IFT proteins (e.g., IFT88), and BBSome components (e.g., BBS4) represent candidate upstream biomarkers of AD. These molecules reflect early dysfunction in ciliary signaling hubs that regulate cAMP production (AC3‐dependent pathways), 262 Hedgehog signaling (SMO/GPR161), 263 Ca2 + homeostasis (polycystin‐mediated), 264 and GPCR trafficking (BBSome‐dependent). 265 Disruption of these pathways is mechanistically linked to impaired synaptic plasticity, altered neuronal excitability, and network vulnerability, which are hypothesized to precede tau aggregation, axonal degeneration, and gliosis. As blood‐based biomarkers, these candidates could be quantified in cEV fractions isolated from plasma and used as adjuncts to established blood‐based AD biomarkers such as p‐tau, Aβ42/40 ratio, neurofilament light chain (NfL), and GFAP. 266 , 267 In a multimodal framework, elevated or dysregulated cEV signatures may identify preclinical or prodromal AD, while conventional markers confirm downstream neurodegenerative burden.

To benchmark cEVs against current blood biomarkers, studies should be designed as head‐to‐head comparisons measuring plasma Aβ42/40, p‐tau181/217, GFAP, and NfL alongside cEV‐derived protein/lipid panels in the same participants and timepoints. Essential performance metrics must encompass diagnostic accuracy (AUCs) for amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) and tau PET positivity, stage sensitivity across preclinical, mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia stages, lead time in relation to clinical conversion, and incremental value beyond standard markers using multivariable models that integrate net reclassification improvement and likelihood‐ratio testing. Biological specificity should further be assessed in common confounder cohorts including vascular cognitive impairment, other tauopathies, and systemic inflammatory states.

A rigorous experimental pipeline would also include longitudinal sampling to define temporal ordering specifically, whether cEV signatures shift before plasma p‐tau and GFAP rise. Perturbation experiments in iPSC‐derived neurons/astrocytes/microglia and AD mouse models, would establish causality between ciliary signaling disruption and cEV cargo remodeling. Ultimately, treatment–response studies will evaluate whether cEV profiles serve as pharmacodynamic biomarkers for cilia/GPCR‐modulating therapies. While low abundance and marker validation remain key hurdles, immunocapture‐based enrichment coupled to ultrasensitive detection provides a feasible translational path, and the central advantage remains that cEVs are poised to offer earlier, cell‐type‐resolved, and pathway‐specific readouts complementing existing blood tests that primarily reflect downstream aggregation or generic neurodegeneration.

CONCLUSION AND PERSPECTIVE
PCs serve critical functions by regulating key signaling pathways involved in neurodevelopment and are associated with various neurological disorders. Dysfunction of these cilia is linked to AD, leading to impaired signal transduction, amyloid clearance, and tau phosphorylation, exacerbating neuroinflammation and synaptic dysfunction. Numerous research studies examining the role of neuronal PCs have elucidated the significance of targeting cilia and elucidated signaling in the treatment of neurological disorders. 268 Nonetheless, our comprehension of the mechanisms related to damage in other cell types, including glial cells, remains inadequate. Accumulating data suggest that PC‐mediated communication in glial cells may be intricately associated with the etiology of several neurological disorders. 163 The well‐established involvement of EVs in aging and age‐related brain diseases implies that they might mediate ciliary signaling pathway activation. 269 , 270 Furthermore, ciliary signaling, PCs, and EVs might all play a role in intercellular communication. 271 Emphasizing cilia‐derived EV subpopulations provides a more sensitive and pathway‐specific insight into early ciliary dysfunction, synaptic impairment, and neuroinflammatory signaling. As a result, cEVs hold immense potential as next‐generation biomarkers enabling earlier detection, efficient disease classification, and more accurate evaluation of neurodegenerative disease progression. To comprehend the fundamental mechanisms of EV‐mediated ciliary signaling in AD, additional investigations are required. This review elucidates recent advances regarding PCs to enhance comprehension of cilia‐mediated AD progression. Finally, it should be noted that PCs are an important but little‐known component of AD pathogenesis. By delving deeper into the intricacies of ciliary signaling, researchers may find new therapeutic targets and diagnostic biomarkers, which may ultimately aid in the development of effective AD therapies.

AUTHOR CONTRIBUTIONS
VSG and CNW conceived the idea. VSG and CNW designed and wrote the paper. CNW had primary responsibility for the final content. All authors read and approved the final manuscript.

The authors declare no conflicts of interest. Author disclosures are available in the Supporting Information.
